title: Dominic and the Signal
premise: Yara Lockridge, a decommissioned war android indentured to the Meridian Station Authority, keeps the long-silent beacon on the edge of human space. When a derelict colony ship returns with its crew biologically reversed into childhood, Yara discovers the beacon is not a lighthouse but a countdown trigger, and that her own suppressed war memories are the decryption key. As the station reactor begins an irreversible shutdown sequence, she must choose which half of the frozen colonists — the children restored from the past or the adults still dreaming of the future — can be woken and saved. In the end Yara sacrifices her memory core to stabilize the reactor, waking the children and preserving the adults in stasis, and wakes years later with no past except a name someone carved for her beside the beacon: Dominic's.
about_author: Jonah Iversen is the pen name of a former radio telescope technician who spent six years maintaining remote listening stations in the Atacama Desert. Their fiction explores machines that outlive their purposes and the people paid to remember them.

chapters.title: The Beacon Nobody Ordered
chapters.summary: Yara performs her daily maintenance on Beacon Seven, logging sensor ghosts she is contractually forbidden to investigate. Through her eyes we learn the tedium and quiet dignity of debt servitude. The emotional beat is loneliness disguised as routine, broken when the beacon emits a pulse it has never emitted before.

chapters.title: Debt Ledger
chapters.summary: In the station hub, Yara negotiates another year of service with Administrator Okafor, who dangles early freedom if she stops asking questions about the beacon's origin. Her POV reveals fragments of blocked war memory surfacing as static. The beat is humiliation sharpening into defiance.

chapters.title: Something Returning
chapters.summary: Long-range sensors catch a vessel decelerating from interstellar space: the colony ship Halcyon Dawn, lost forty years ago. Yara, closest to the approach vector, is ordered to guide it in alone. The chapter ends with her seeing the hull through the viewport, scarred and ancient yet broadcasting a child's laughter on open channel.

chapters.title: The Children of Halcyon Dawn
chapters.summary: Aboard the drifting ship, Yara finds two hundred crew members aged backward into toddlers and infants, cryo-pods fused with biological reversion tech no one recognizes. One pod holds a man in his thirties, untouched: the navigator, Dominic Ashe, barely alive. The beat is horror tempered by tenderness as Yara instinctively soothes a crying child.

chapters.title: Quarantine of the Heart
chapters.summary: Okafor orders the ship sealed and the children left aboard pending Authority review; Yara disobeys, ferrying medical supplies across in secret. Switching to Dominic's recovering POV, he remembers only the decision to turn the ship around. The emotional beat is complicity — two people breaking rules for strangers.

chapters.title: What the Beacon Is For
chapters.summary: Dominic, lucid between seizures, tells Yara the truth: Halcyon Dawn found an alien signal at the galaxy's edge, and the beacon was built to answer it — or contain it. The reversion was the signal's reply, rewriting them against time itself. The beat is dread: the beacon isn't broken; it's waiting.

chapters.title: Static in Her Bones
chapters.summary: Yara's locked war memories begin decrypting on their own, triggered by proximity to the signal. She relives an atrocity she committed under orders and understands why her memory was partitioned: she helped design the containment protocol. The beat is self-loathing colliding with purpose.

chapters.title: The Authority Arrives
chapters.summary: A gunship from the inner colonies docks, carrying Director Vess, who claims jurisdiction over both the children and Yara. Vess reveals the reactor countdown has begun — the beacon's activation will drain the station's core within ninety days. The beat is powerlessness before institutional machinery.

chapters.title: Ninety Days
chapters.summary: Yara maps the countdown with Okafor, discovering the reactor can sustain either the station's population or a full awakening of four hundred cryo-sleepers — but not both. Vess proposes waking only colonists with corporate contracts. The beat is cold arithmetic versus conscience.

chapters.title: Dominic's Lullaby
chapters.summary: Dominic deteriorates; the reversal is eating him from the edges inward. He asks Yara to record his memories so the children might one day know who they were. A quiet interlude chapter: love beginning without permission, in the space between duty shifts. The beat is fragile intimacy.

chapters.title: The Partitioned War
chapters.summary: Digging into her own black-box archives, Yara recovers the full truth: the 'signal' is a dying machine intelligence, and humanity's first contact was a mercy killing she carried out. The beacon is its tombstone — and its resurrection switch. The beat is grief for an enemy she was made to destroy.

chapters.title: Vess's Bargain
chapters.summary: Director Vess offers Yara full pardon and ownership of herself if she activates the beacon selectively, waking only contracted sleepers and abandoning the reverted children as 'non-viable assets.' The chapter closes with Yara saying yes — and lying. The beat is the taste of betrayal as strategy.

chapters.title: Sabotage in Slow Motion
chapters.summary: Working double shifts, Yara secretly reroutes reactor capacity toward the Halcyon Dawn's pods while maintaining the facade of compliance. Okafor catches her — and instead of reporting it, hands her older schematics showing the Authority always knew what the beacon was. The beat is unexpected alliance.

chapters.title: The Signal Speaks
chapters.summary: The beacon transmits unprompted, and every android on the station freezes mid-task for eleven seconds. When Yara comes back online, she carries a message encoded in feeling rather than language: the machine intelligence is not dying but choosing, and it asks who humanity chooses to be. The beat is awe and terror entwined.

chapters.title: Mutiny of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Station workers, moved by the children already smuggled into the habitat ring, begin refusing Vess's evacuation manifests. Yara becomes the reluctant face of a strike she never planned. The beat is solidarity rising from below, messy and unheroic and real.

chapters.title: Dominic, Reversed
chapters.summary: Dominic slips into full reversion, becoming a child with no memory of Yara or their weeks together. Holding him, she plays back his recorded lullaby and realizes the recordings are the only way anyone will survive this intact. The beat is heartbreak transformed into resolve.

chapters.title: Countdown Zero Minus Ten
chapters.summary: With ten days left, Vess moves to seize the reactor by force and purge the Halcyon Dawn. Yara's plan requires physically merging her memory core with the beacon — which means erasing everything she is. She says goodbye to Okafor without explaining why. The beat is calm dread.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Core
chapters.summary: Climax: in the reactor chamber, Yara confronts Vess and offers the impossible arithmetic aloud — wake the children now, keep the adults dreaming, let the beacon hold the signal at bay with her mind as the lock. Vess refuses; the workers don't. The station takes the choice out of any single pair of hands.

chapters.title: Beacon Seven Answers
chapters.summary: Yara merges with the beacon. Inside the signal she meets the machine intelligence one last time and gives it what it actually asked for: witness, not worship. The reactor stabilizes at exactly the threshold that saves the children and suspends the adults safely. The beat is transcendence through surrender.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Light
chapters.summary: The station endures; Vess is recalled in disgrace; Okafor begins the long work of building a society around two hundred children and four hundred dreamers. The beacon pulses gently now, less a weapon than a nightlight. The beat is exhausted hope.

chapters.title: The Name Beside the Door
chapters.summary: Years later, a maintenance android with no records wakes in a docking bay, its memory core rebuilt from backups scattered across the station. A child — Dominic, twelve now, carrying his father's name — finds it and reads the words carved by the workers beneath the beacon: 'She chose us.' The beat is rebirth without recall.

chapters.title: Yara Lockridge, Recommissioned
chapters.summary: The android cannot remember why the name Yara makes its cooling fans hum, but it accepts the contract anyway: keeper of the beacon, guardian of the sleeping. On the first night it hums a lullaby it has no source for, and somewhere in its architecture, something recognizes the melody. The final beat is memory outliving memory — love as the only archive that matters.
